title: Episode 294: Stephen and Empress Matilda: The Anarchy: Nineteen Winters of Blood When Christ Slept

The chaotic, devastating, and epic saga of The Anarchy: the nineteen-year civil war between King Stephen of Blois and his cousin, Empress Matilda, for the crown of England. Following the death of Henry I in 1135, Stephen broke his sacred oath and seized the crown, igniting a brutal dynastic feud that tore England apart. Chronicled in the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle as nineteen winters when 'Christ and His saints slept', robber barons constructed illegal adulterine castles, tortured peasants for ransom, and ravaged the shires. Featuring Matilda's daring white-shrouded escape across the frozen River Thames at Oxford, Stephen's capture at the Battle of Lincoln, and the eventual Treaty of Wallingford elevating Matilda's son Henry II to the throne, discover the darkest winter of English royalty.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Today, our Kings and Queens of England series explores the darkest chapter of the Norman era: the brutal civil war between cousins that shattered the realm, described by chroniclers as a time when heaven seemed to turn its back on England. Here is George with the extraordinary story of Stephen and Empress Matilda.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: THE STOLEN CROWN AND THE USURPATION OF STEPHEN: DECEMBER 1135
When Henry I died in Normandy in December 1135, his daughter Empress Matilda was in Anjou with her unpopular French husband, Count Geoffrey Plantagenet, paralyzed by political disputes. Seizing the moment, Henry's affable, charismatic nephew, Count Stephen of Blois—who had been the very first baron to swear allegiance to Matilda in 1127—raced across the winter Channel to England. London's wealthy merchant aldermen, fearing foreign Angevin rule, embraced Stephen, and with the assistance of his brother, Bishop Henry of Winchester, Stephen seized the royal treasury and was crowned King of England at Westminster Abbey on December 26, 1135. Stephen was courageous and generous, but fatally weak in judgment and lacking the ruthless iron resolve required to govern Norman barons, handing out vast royal estates, titles, and minting privileges to buy aristocratic loyalty.  Stephen of Blois was the son of the Conqueror's daughter Adela and Count Stephen of Blois, a gallant and courteous prince whose generous smile, athletic grace, and accessibility to ordinary folk made him beloved by the London citizenry. But Stephen's fatal flaw was his complete inability to say no: in his desperate bid to secure the crown before Empress Matilda could cross the Channel, Stephen squandered the vast royal treasure accumulated by Henry I, showering baron after baron with royal charters, earldoms, and castles in exchange for hollow promises of loyalty. When the powerful Bishop Roger of Salisbury and his kin began fortifying private castles, Stephen made the catastrophic blunder of arresting them, alienating the powerful English Church and turning his own brother, Bishop Henry of Winchester, into a bitter political enemy.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: THE EMPRESS STRIKES: ROBERT OF GLOUCESTER AND THE INVASION OF 1139
Empress Matilda, daughter of an emperor and a king, possessed an imperious, unbending pride and a ferocious determination to reclaim her lawful inheritance. In 1138, her illegitimate half-brother, Robert, Earl of Gloucester—the wealthiest and most formidable military commander in England—renounced his fealty to Stephen, declaring for the Empress. In September 1139, Matilda landed on the coast of Sussex with a small invasion force, establishing her headquarters at Bristol Castle. England fractured into two hostile armed camps: Stephen held London, East Anglia, and the south-east, while Matilda and Earl Robert dominated the West Country, the Welsh Marches, and the south-west, setting the stage for a grinding, bloody war of attrition.  Empress Matilda arrived on English shores possessing the haughty, imperial demeanor of a Holy Roman Empress: widow of Emperor Henry V, she signed her charters 'Matilda the Empress' and viewed the crown of England as her inalienable divine right. Her half-brother Robert, Earl of Gloucester, was the military anchor of her cause: a brilliant, incorruptible general whose vast estates in Wales, Gloucestershire, and Normandy gave the Angevin faction an unassailable western redoubt. The war quickly degenerated into a brutal patchwork of regional sieges: while Stephen marched back and forth across the Midlands playing an exhausting game of military whack-a-mole, Matilda's supporters consolidated their grip on Bristol, Gloucester, and the Welsh borders.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: THE BATTLE OF LINCOLN AND THE CAPTIVE KING: FEBRUARY 1141
On February 2, 1141, the rival factions met in a rare, bloody pitched battle outside the stone walls of Lincoln Castle. While many of Stephen's cowardly earls fled early in the engagement, King Stephen fought in the center with suicidal bravery: wielding a heavy Danish battle-axe until it shattered in his hands, he drew his broadsword and fought on until the blade was broken, finally being struck down by a stone and captured by Earl Robert's men. Dragged in chains to Bristol Castle, Stephen was locked in a dark stone cell. Empress Matilda entered London in triumph, proclaimed 'Lady of the English' by a church council at Winchester, preparing for her coronation at Westminster Abbey. Her dynastic triumph appeared absolute.  The Battle of Lincoln on February 2, 1141, was a spectacle of raw feudal ferocity: King Stephen had besieged Lincoln Castle to punish the rebellious Earl Ranulf of Chester, when Earl Robert of Gloucester arrived with a relief army of Angevin cavalry and disinherited Welsh infantry. When Stephen's cavalry flanks broke and fled early in the engagement, the king was left isolated in the center with a small circle of royal bodyguards. Stephen fought like a mythic berserker: his heavy battle-axe clove through helmets and chainmail until it shattered against an enemy shield, whereupon he drew his broadsword and fought until the blade snapped in two, standing defiant until struck down by a heavy stone. Imprisoned in chains at Bristol, Stephen's crown was laid at the feet of the triumphant Empress.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: THE WRATH OF LONDON AND THE LADY DRIVEN OUT: JUNE 1141
Matilda's triumph collapsed within weeks due to her haughty arrogance and political tone-deafness. When the wealthy citizens of London petitioned the Empress to lower taxes and confirm the ancient laws of Edward the Confessor, Matilda treated them with contempt, imperiously demanding crushing financial tallages. Simultaneously, Stephen's devoted and brilliant queen—also named Matilda, Queen of England—mobilized a royalist army in Kent and advanced on the capital. On June 24, 1141, just as the banquet tables were being set for the Empress's coronation at Westminster, London church bells rang the alarm: thousands of armed citizens poured into the streets with spears and clubs, swarming the palace. The Empress and her retainers fled for their lives on horseback, abandoning their dinner and leaving London in a humiliating, panicked gallop.  Empress Matilda's failure to secure her coronation in June 1141 was one of the most stunning political self-destructions in British history: entering London with arrogant disdain, she refused to grant the city its ancient charters, demanded ruinous financial tallages from the merchant guilds, and publicly insulted the citizens who begged for mercy. Stephen's queen, Queen Matilda—a woman of extraordinary courage, intelligence, and military grit—rallied the royalist barons of Kent and Surrey, marching her army to the south bank of the Thames. When London's church bells tolled in rebellion and armed mobs swarmed Westminster Palace, the Empress was forced to leap onto her horse and gallop away in disgrace, leaving her coronation banquet to be looted by the furious London citizenry.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: THE ROUT OF WINCHESTER AND THE EXCHANGE OF PRISONERS: SEPTEMBER 1141
Fleeing to Winchester, the Empress attempted to besiege Bishop Henry of Winchester's fortress, only to be surrounded by Queen Matilda's royalist cavalry in a deadly trap known as the 'Rout of Winchester'. While Empress Matilda escaped disguised on a horse, her military commander Earl Robert of Gloucester was captured covering her retreat. The civil war had reached a bizarre, paradoxical stalemate: the rebels held the King in chains at Bristol, while the royalists held the leader of the rebellion in captivity at Rochester. In November 1141, the only logical solution was negotiated: Stephen was traded for Earl Robert, returning the conflict to square one with neither side possessing the strength to deliver a decisive blow.  The 'Rout of Winchester' in September 1141 was a chaotic military disaster for the Angevin cause: besieging the bishop's palace inside the city, the Empress's forces were suddenly encircled by Queen Matilda's royalist cavalry, who set fire to the city and trapped the Angevins between burning churches and advancing lances. While Empress Matilda escaped disguised in a peasant's cart and rode through the night to Devizes, Earl Robert of Gloucester was captured by William of Ypres' Flemish mercenaries while defending the river crossing at Stockbridge. The resulting prisoner exchange in November 1141 restored King Stephen to his throne, leaving both factions exhausted and cementing a brutal, unwinnable stalemate that tore the country apart for another decade.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE WHITE CLOAK OF OXFORD AND NINETEEN WINTERS OF BLOOD: 1142 TO 1152
In December 1142, Stephen trapped Empress Matilda inside Oxford Castle, maintaining a starving siege through a freezing winter. With food exhausted and surrender imminent, Matilda engineered one of the most daring escapes in medieval history: draped in a white linen cloak to blend into the falling snow, she was lowered by ropes from the castle tower with three loyal knights at midnight. Walking silently past sleeping royalist sentries, she stepped onto the frozen River Thames, crossing the ice and trekking six miles through blinding blizzards to safety at Wallingford. Meanwhile, across England, law and order completely disintegrated. Barons constructed hundreds of unlicensed 'adulterine' castles, minting their own counterfeit coin, torturing peasants with thumbscrews and knotted cords to extort gold, and burning villages. As the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle recorded in despair: 'Men said openly that Christ and His saints slept.'  Matilda's midnight escape from Oxford Castle in December 1142 was a legend of courage and cunning: with royalist siege lines encircling the city and starvation consuming the garrison, Matilda and three loyal knights cloaked themselves in white linen bedsheets, slipping down a rope from the castle tower into the blinding winter blizzard. Creeping past sleeping Norman sentries, they stepped onto the frozen surface of the River Thames, walking six miles across the ice to Abingdon before mounting horses to safety at Wallingford. Meanwhile, across England, the horrors of the Anarchy deepened: robber barons like Geoffrey de Mandeville turned the Fens into an armed wasteland, building adulterine castles, hanging peasants by their feet over smoking fires, and looting monasteries, turning England into a living hell of famine, banditry, and blood.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE TREATY OF WALLINGFORD AND THE DAWN OF THE PLANTAGENETS: 1153 AND LEGACY
The grueling deadlock was finally broken by a new generation: Matilda's charismatic, dynamic son, Henry Plantagenet, Duke of Normandy. Landing in England in 1153, young Henry outmaneuvered Stephen's demoralized forces. When Stephen's arrogant eldest son and heir, Eustace, died suddenly in August 1153—choking to death on a plundered monastic meal—the grief-stricken king lost the will to fight. In November 1153, the rival leaders met on the banks of the Thames, signing the Treaty of Wallingford: Stephen was permitted to reign as king for the rest of his natural life, on the condition that he adopt young Henry as his son and legal successor. Less than a year later, in October 1154, King Stephen died, ending nineteen winters of civil war and inaugurating the glorious three-century reign of the Plantagenet dynasty under King Henry II.  The Anarchy was finally brought to an end by the emergence of Empress Matilda's son, young Henry Plantagenet, who invaded England in 1153 with a disciplined army and the vast wealth of Normandy and Aquitaine. When the exhausted royalist and Angevin armies met face-to-face across the River Thames at Wallingford, the barons on both sides flatly refused to fight, demanding a negotiated settlement to end nineteen years of fratricidal slaughter. The sudden death of Stephen's ruthless heir Eustace broke the king's spirit, leading to the historic Treaty of Wallingford: Stephen reigned as king until his death in October 1154, passing the English crown peacefully to Henry II. The Anarchy proved the absolute necessity of strong, centralized royal justice, clearing the stage for the glorious legal and constitutional triumphs of the Plantagenet era.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
Thank you for listening to Most Fascinating Stories. The drama of The Anarchy and the endurance of Empress Matilda paved the way for England's greatest medieval dynasty. Join us next week as Rebecca returns with the colossal builder of the Angevin Empire: King Henry II, the Common Law, and the murder of Thomas Becket. Until then, stay curious.
